headline: Italy fines Meta for accessing users' phone photos

sources.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos (BBC News)
Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users' photos and videos (The Guardian)
Italy hits Meta with €805m fine over privacy law violation (Politico Europe)

chunks.text: On November 14, 2026, Italy's Data Protection Authority {{handed out}} a [[fine]] of 805 million euros, or about 887 million dollars, to Meta, Facebook's owner. A fine is money paid as a punishment. The agency, which protects [[personal information]], said Facebook's Android phone app used people's photos and videos without their [[specific]] [[consent]], meaning clear permission for that exact use. When setting the fine, it {{factored in}} the roughly 20 million people affected in Italy.

verbs.wrong: To write a new law for schools
verbs.why: Police officers hand out tickets to drivers who speed. The judge hands out a tough punishment to the thief. Italy's Data Protection Authority handed out a fine to Meta.

verbs.wrong: To send data to another agency
verbs.why: Good drivers factor in the traffic when they leave home. Banks factor in your income before they give a loan. The agency factored in the roughly 20 million people affected in Italy.

chunks.text: The case is about a feature that Meta {{rolled out}} in 2023. While people [[browse]] Facebook, the feature {{picks out}} saved photos and videos from their phone's [[gallery]] as ideas for posts. Facebook asked for one [[permission]] covering the whole app. The agency said the message that {{popped up}} was too general. It did not {{spell out}} that the app would use people's photos for [[suggestions]]. The agency says users who {{went along with}} the request could not understand this.

verbs.correct: To make a new feature available
verbs.wrong: To report a feature to the police
verbs.why: Phone makers roll out new features every fall. Our bank rolls out a new app every few years. Meta rolled out the photo feature in 2023.
The app picks out the best photos from each trip. My mom picks out a few good apples at the store. The feature picks out photos and videos from a phone's gallery.

verbs.correct: To appear suddenly on a screen
verbs.wrong: To send a warning by email
verbs.why: A warning pops up when my battery is low. Ads often pop up while I read the news. The agency said the message that popped up was too general.

verbs.wrong: To translate a message for users
verbs.why: Good contracts spell out every cost. My boss spells out exactly what she wants. The message did not spell out that Facebook would use people's photos for suggestions.

verbs.correct: To accept a request or plan
verbs.wrong: To pay extra for an app
verbs.why: I often go along with my friends' plans for the weekend. Most workers go along with the new rules. The agency says users who went along with the request could not understand it.

chunks.text: The agency said this permission can let an app read a phone's whole [[photo archive]], usually [[permanently]]. It said the problem is still {{going on}} for people who have not updated the app. The agency began {{looking into}} the feature in 2025. It {{called out}} Meta's [[lack of cooperation]] during the investigation. The fine equals about 0.4 percent of Meta's [[yearly sales]]. It is one of Italy's largest fines for a tech company.

verbs.wrong: To be sent to a court
verbs.why: The noise from the bar goes on all night. Our team meetings often go on for hours. The problem is still going on for people who have not updated the app.

verbs.correct: To study a problem to learn the facts
verbs.wrong: To build a feature for a new phone
verbs.why: The police look into every complaint they get. The school looks into the problem when a parent calls. The agency began looking into the feature in 2025.

verbs.wrong: To print a letter on paper
verbs.why: Fans call out the coach when the team plays badly. Customers often call out companies for bad service online. The agency called out Meta's lack of cooperation during the investigation.

chunks.text: Meta has 60 days to {{turn the feature off}} [[by default]], so it stays off unless a user chooses it. Meta must ask for consent just for this feature. Meta {{pushed back}}. A [[spokesperson]] said Meta strongly disagrees and called the fine [[disproportionate]], or too large. Meta says people give permission on their phones and can change it in [[settings]]. Meta plans to [[appeal]], or ask for the decision to be changed.

verbs.correct: To stop a feature from working
verbs.wrong: To move a feature to a new app
verbs.why: Many people turn off the sound on their phones at night. I turn off location tracking when I do not need it. Meta has 60 days to turn the feature off by default.

verbs.correct: To say you oppose a decision
verbs.wrong: To delete a user's old posts
verbs.why: Workers push back when the boss cuts their pay. Parents often push back against new school rules. After the decision, Meta pushed back.

mainIdea.s: Italy's privacy agency fined Meta 805 million euros over a Facebook feature that used photos on Android phones. It says users never gave clear permission, but Meta disagrees and plans to appeal.
mainIdea.why: The agency says a general message did not spell out that the app would use people's photos. Meta pushed back and plans to appeal.

mainIdea.s: An Italian regulator punished Meta because Facebook secretly sold private pictures to advertisers. As a result, the company must now remove all of these images from its servers within two months.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nothing was sold to advertisers. The problem was that a feature picks out photos from a phone's gallery without clear consent.

mainIdea.s: Lawmakers in Rome have passed a new rule that bans children under 14 from joining social media apps. Parents who ignore this rule could pay large penalties, and the ban starts next spring.
mainIdea.why: No new law was passed. The agency handed out a fine to Meta because Facebook's Android app used people's photos without clear consent.

tf.s: Users went along with one request that covered the whole app.

tf.s: The agency says the problem has ended for every user.
tf.why: The problem still goes on for people who have not updated the app, the agency says.

tf.why: Meta has 60 days to turn the feature off by default and ask for consent just for this feature.

tf.s: Meta accepted the decision and did not push back.
tf.why: Meta pushed back hard. It strongly disagrees, calls the fine too large and plans to appeal.

lines.text: Did you hear that Italy {{handed out}} a huge fine to Meta?
I saw that. Eight hundred and five million euros, right? What did Facebook do?
It's about a feature that {{picks out}} photos from your phone's gallery and suggests them for posts.
Meta {{rolled out}} the feature in 2023, and the agency started {{looking into}} it in 2025.
I think I've seen it. I tap yes on those permission messages [[without a second thought]].
That's what the agency says. The message that {{popped up}} didn't {{spell out}} what the permission was for.
So people {{went along with}} it and gave the app access to all their photos without knowing it.
That's the agency's view. A lot of us do say yes [[out of habit]].
How did they get such a big number?
They {{factored in}} the twenty million people affected. And the problem is still {{going on}} for anyone who hasn't updated the app.
What does Meta have to do now?
It has sixty days to {{turn the feature off}} by default and ask people separately.
Meta can't be happy about that.
No, it {{pushed back}} hard. It says people can change the permission in their settings at any time.
Sure, but most people never check their settings. [[Case in point]]: me.
Well, [[when in doubt]], say no. You can always say yes later.
True. [[It never hurts]] to check what your apps can see.
